analysis:
The PR adds an operator-selected model filter (`operatorModelFilter`, ProviderLoop.swift head lines 221-224, 946-948). The filter is seeded from `enabled_models` plus the start selection, and is nil when `enabled_models` is empty. In ProviderLoop+Prefetch.swift `reconcileDesiredModels`, a coordinator-declared successor build is now added to `ordinaryServingModelIDs` only if `operatorFilterAllows(entry.desiredBuild)` passes (head line 353). The desired-models loop also logs and skips builds outside the filter (head 382-388). Both changes narrow what the coordinator can push onto the provider, so they tighten rather than weaken the consumed-contract boundary (TB-002) and the provider's serving availability (A-018). The coordinator remains trusted, but a stale or compromised desired_models push can no longer auto-expand the ordinary serving set beyond the operator's selection.

I found no new exposure to plaintext, keys, attestation or authorization. The change touches only model-selection policy and logging; the logged strings are model names and builds, not secrets.

Open integration questions, outside the supplied evidence:
- The implementations of `operatorFilterAllows` and `autopilotAllowsModel` are not shown. I did not verify that `autopilotAllowsModel` applies the operator filter on every path, including `handlePrefetchModelRequest` and the autopilot download path. I also did not verify that live model-switch code updates `operatorModelFilter`; the comment says it does, but those callers are not in this diff.
- With a nil filter, any coordinator-pushed model is served. This is the previous behavior and not a regression.
- A stale `operatorModelFilter` after a live switch would at worst cause under-serving (a DoS-like availability effect), not disclosure.

The diff shows no concrete regression.
